title: Jansenius: grace physically predetermines the will
source_text: XLII. Imo idem ille cum Thomistis asserit, huic Christi adjutorio vere competere officium voluntatem physice praedeterminandi. Quippe tale illud esse ut voluntatem ad actum pertrahat, non si voluerit, sed ei efficacissime praebendo ut velit. Quoniam non expectat ut voluntas secum influat, sed facit secum influere voluntatem, applicans eam ad volendum agendumque, quicquid per eam Deus volendum agendumque constituerit. Cum enim per terrenas cupiditates, ut ait, voluntas ad non volendum, imo ad repugnandum determinata sit; tollit istam depressionem, atque determinationem in contrarium, & reflectit eam in bonum, non solum si libero arbitrio hoc videatur, & velit; sed ineffabili sua luce atque suavitate, faciendo ut ei sic videatur, & velit. Sic Deus, juxta ipsum, ex nolentibus & repugnantibus volentes & consentientes facit; voluntatem, scilicet, inclinando, applicando, determinando, & quia praevenit ipsam voluntatis determinationem, etiam praedeterminando; non solum moraliter, sed vera, reali & physica determinatione. Quoniam moralis praedeterminatio illa dicitur quae tantum se habet ex parte objecti, & per modum allicientis, blandientis, rogantis, consulentis &c. sive extrinsecus, sive intrinsecus; sed haec se habet in ipsa potentia voluntatis, quam proprie suae suavitatis magnitudine ad volendum applicat, & applicando determinat, utpote causans in ea hoc ipsum ut se determinet, ideoque praedeterminat. De gratia Christi salvatoris lib. 8. cap. 3.
pass_a_gloss: XLII. Nay the same man asserts with the Thomists, that to this help of Christ truly belongs the office of physically predetermining the will. Since it is such that it draws the will to act, not if it wills, but by most efficaciously furnishing to it that it will. Because it does not wait that the will flow in with it, but makes the will flow in with it, applying it to willing and doing, whatever God has determined to be willed and done through it. For since through earthly desires, as he says, the will has been determined to not willing, nay to resisting; it takes away that depression, and determination to the contrary, and bends it back to good, not only if it seems so to free choice, and it wills; but by its ineffable light and sweetness, making that it so seem to it, and it will. Thus God, according to him, from the unwilling and resisting makes willing and consenting; namely, by inclining, applying, determining the will, and because it forestalls the very determination of the will, also by predetermining; not only morally, but by a true, real and physical determination. Since that is called moral predetermination which only holds itself on the part of the object, and by way of one alluring, flattering, asking, counselling etc. whether outwardly, or inwardly; but this holds itself in the very power of the will, which properly by the greatness of its sweetness it applies to willing, and by applying determines, as causing in it this very thing that it determine itself, and therefore predetermines. On the grace of Christ the saviour book 8. chap. 3.
pass_b_english: Thesis XLII. Indeed Jansenius asserts with the Thomists that the task of physically predetermining the will truly belongs to this aid of Christ. It is such that it draws the will to act, not if the will chooses, but by most effectively granting it to will. It does not wait for the will to act together with it; it makes the will act together with it, applying the will to will and do whatever God has resolved should be willed and done through it.

For since, as he says, the will has been set by earthly desires toward not willing, and even toward resisting, this aid removes that downward pull and that bent in the opposite direction and turns the will back toward the good, not merely if free choice sees fit and wills, but by its own inexpressible light and sweetness, causing it to see fit and to will. So, on his account, God makes willing and consenting people out of unwilling and resisting ones, by inclining, applying and determining the will, and, because he anticipates the will's own determination, by predetermining it too: not only morally but by a true, real and physical determination.

For moral predetermination is the kind that works only from the side of the object, by way of something that allures, coaxes, asks, counsels and so on, whether from outside or within. This predetermination, by contrast, works in the will's power itself, which it properly applies to willing by the greatness of its sweetness, and by applying it determines it, since it causes in the will this very act of determining itself, and therefore predetermines it. De gratia Christi Salvatoris, book 8, chapter 3.
